synthesis.headline: Quiet Tuesday; a northern Plains low deepens east, bringing wind, Ohio Valley storms and a cold shot
synthesis.narrative:
There is no severe weather today and no excessive-rainfall risk on Day 1 or Day 2. The story is the next 48 hours: a modest 1011 mb low on the northern Plains stationary front dives southeast and deepens into a strong eastern storm by Thursday. The South Texas cutoff that brought the heavy rain is now a weak shortwave easing toward the lower Mississippi Valley. It leaves Gulf Coast showers and elevated thunderstorms along coastal Texas and Louisiana, but with MUCAPE under 1000 J/kg any hail stays below severe size. Weak 1020-1026 mb highs keep the interior calm and mild. Activity sits at the edges. A 956 mb occluded low offshore gives the Pacific Northwest the map's tightest gradient, with rain and mountain snow (a few inches on the Olympic Peninsula through Thursday). In eastern Canada, a 995 mb low trails a cold front toward the Great Lakes and Northeast.

Aloft, a fast, low-amplitude westerly belt (50-70 kt at 500 mb) runs from the northern Rockies to the Northeast. The weak southern low sits detached beneath it, so the flow is split, not blocked. Its center near 588 dam marks it as shallow and warm, not a cold-core cutoff. The energy that matters is the cold upper air (deep purple on Air Mass RGB) over the Northwest and northern Rockies, with a cloud band across Montana and the Dakotas. That trough digs into the mid-Mississippi Valley Wednesday. Ahead of it, mid-50s dewpoints and about 50 kt of deep-layer shear support a few damaging gusts, held back by poor lapse rates. Behind it, cold air surges east Wednesday night. Expect wet snow in the upper Great Lakes by Thursday morning and strong winds across the East as the low reaches the Appalachians.

The trough closes off over the East Friday into Saturday, bringing:
- cold, windy rain from the Mid-Atlantic to the Northeast
- the season's first lake-effect rain and snow
- upslope snow in West Virginia and western Maryland
- highs 5-15 F below average from the Southeast to the central Appalachians
- the first widespread frost and freeze from the interior Deep South to the Ohio Valley

The West turns wet: 1-2 inches of rain Friday from northern California to western Washington, then lower Sierra snow levels. South Texas could see heavy rain this weekend from a southern-stream trough. A High Plains ridge keeps the Plains mild. CPC's 6-10 day chart centers the warmth over central Canada and the Great Lakes, with 80-90% odds of above normal in the Dakotas and Minnesota. By 8-14 days that warmth moves to the Great Lakes and Northeast while troughing settles over the West, so the eastern cold looks short-lived.
synthesis.climate_context: A strong, still-strengthening El Niño frames the season. The Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.46°C for August-October, up from -0.21°C in January-March and rising about 0.3°C per season lately. An active southern jet stream is typical of strong El Niño cool seasons. Last week's South Texas cutoff and the southern-stream trough expected this weekend fit that pattern, though one week proves nothing. NHC expects no Atlantic development in the next 7 days as the season winds down. Far to the west, Tropical Storm Pena (35 kt, 1004 mb) is moving west at 14 mph about 770 miles south-southwest of Honolulu. It should pass well south of Johnston Atoll with no land hazards and may weaken to a remnant low. Teleconnection indices haven't updated since October 31, so they aren't used here.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has a Day 2 Marginal risk for the lower Ohio and western Tennessee Valleys. Storms should form late Wednesday afternoon near the Mississippi-Ohio confluence and spread into southern Indiana, western Kentucky and northern Tennessee by early evening, with about 500 J/kg MLCAPE and a few severe gusts possible. There are no active mesoscale discussions. Frost advisories cover eastern North Carolina and southeastern Virginia this morning. Low-topped convection on the Washington coast may produce occasional lightning today.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 0900Z analysis (Tue Nov 10) is dominated by a quasi-stationary high-pressure belt across the central and eastern U.S., with weak highs of about 1020-1026 mb scattered from the northern Rockies and Plains through the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast. None is strong enough to be called a dominant anticyclone. The deepest labeled centers are a 1011 mb low near the northern Plains/Canadian border and a 1004 mb low in the western Great Lakes/southern Canada region, with a third low near the Maine/Atlantic Canada edge of the chart. Pressure values of 1004-1011 mb are modest, so these are routine autumn systems rather than intense cyclones.

The key boundary is a long cold front, drawn with blue triangles, running from the northern Plains and Upper Midwest southwest across Nebraska, Kansas, and into the southern Plains of Oklahoma and north Texas, with a stationary or weakly slow-moving segment of mixed symbols near the Lakes. A separate front with alternating red semicircles and blue triangles extends west-to-east along the Canadian border and across Montana, North Dakota, and Minnesota. This is a stationary front, and it appears tied to the 1011 mb low. A trough or weak frontal segment with dashed lines is also visible along the southern Plains and Gulf Coast, but its type is hard to resolve at this resolution.

Pressure gradients are slack across most of the interior: isobars are widely spaced from the Plains to the Appalachians, consistent with light winds and the scattered high centers. The tightest packing is in the Pacific Northwest and along the far northwestern edge of the chart, where several closely spaced isobars appear near the West Coast and a deeper low sits off the chart edge. Some isobar crowding also appears near the northern Great Lakes close to the 1004 mb low.

Surface convergence and lift are focused along the cold front from the southern Plains up through the mid-Mississippi Valley and Great Lakes, where temperatures in the 40s and 50s on the cool side contrast with 60s and 70s ahead of the front along the Gulf Coast and Texas. The Gulf of Mexico and the Southeast carry the warmest, most humid air, with dewpoints near the upper 50s to 60s plotted, so any frontal lift there would tap the best moisture. Beyond what is plotted, any inferences about precipitation or severe weather would need radar and upper-air data.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This CMC surface analysis, valid 00Z Tuesday 10 November 2026, is dominated by a deep, occluded cyclone over the northeast Pacific, centered near 956 mb in the lower-left quadrant. Its occluded and cold fronts wrap well south and east, and a long front runs northeast from the low's vicinity toward the left edge of the continent (Alaska panhandle/British Columbia coast is my best reading, though the coastline is hard to resolve at this scale). The packed isobars around the low show the tightest gradient on the chart, with a secondary low near 972 mb on its western flank.

Farther east, a trailing front sweeps down the Pacific coast and curves back toward the interior west, stretching from the occluded low through the western Canadian interior. Several 1020 to 1030 mb highs sit over the central and northern continent, including a 1029 mb high over the interior and others near the Arctic coast. Gradients are modest under these highs, and the frontal activity over central Canada looks weak by comparison.

On the right side, a 995 mb low sits over eastern Canada with a front to its east and a cold front and trough trailing south toward the Great Lakes and northeastern United States, with another 1006 mb low near the lower Great Lakes. These carry the main focused lift across the eastern cross-border region. Farther east over the North Atlantic, a very deep closed low near 975 mb with a broad circulation dominates the right margin.

At top, in the high Arctic, lows near 976 and 981 mb sit over the Arctic Ocean and archipelago sector, with a front arcing around them. The polar projection compresses this region, so I would place those lows relative to the visible island coastlines rather than assign them to a specific province or territory.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The 500 mb pattern at 1200 UTC 10 Nov shows a fast, nearly zonal westerly belt across the northern tier, with the strongest flow (shaded olive/yellow, roughly 50-70 kt by the scale) in two corridors: one across the northern Rockies and Plains into the Great Lakes, and another across the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic. A second wind maximum appears over the Pacific Northwest and British Columbia, with the darkest shading in the top-left corner. Heights over the northern U.S. run roughly 540-570 dam in a tightly packed contour band, with only modest ridge-trough undulation, so the longwave amplitude is low and the flow is progressive rather than blocked.

The standout feature is a closed 588 dam contour hugging the red L over the southern High Plains, in the Texas Panhandle/western Oklahoma vicinity (placed relative to the visible Texas-Oklahoma-New Mexico borders). Its center sits near 588 dam by the labeled contour, which is a high value for a closed low, and the surrounding height field shows a weak circulation south of the main westerlies. The low is separated from the jet by a broad gap of weak gradient and light winds, so it is detached and likely self-retaining, tending to drift slowly rather than race downstream. Its small closed circulation and sparse wind barbs argue for a modest, shallow cutoff rather than a deep, cold-core system.

South of the cutoff, a separate green-shaded wind maximum over the Gulf of Mexico and the western Gulf coast (around 40-45 kt) suggests a subtropical jet segment, though this is an implied jet corridor from the wind shading, not a plotted axis. Heights of 580-590 dam across Texas and the Gulf indicate a warm, high-height airmass over the southern tier, while the 5400-5600 m range in the north reflects the colder air beneath the main jet.

This is not a Rex block: there is no anticyclone poleward of the cutoff, only a weak-gradient low beneath fast zonal flow to its north. The better description is a quasi-zonal northern jet over a detached southern low, a split-flow configuration. The cutoff's tilt cannot be assessed from a single level, and no distinct shortwave troughs are clearly resolved in the contours aside from slight undulations in the Plains-to-Great Lakes belt.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The most striking feature is a long, sharp airmass boundary arcing from the southern Plains of Texas and Oklahoma eastward along the Tennessee Valley and Carolinas and out over the western Atlantic. Dry orange-brown air lies along and just south of this band, with tropical moist green air to the south over the Gulf, Florida, and Caribbean. The tight color gradient marks the likely jet corridor, with the implied flow running west to east and curving gently southeastward off the Carolina and Georgia coast. This orange band is broad and smooth rather than compact and elongated, so I read it as dry upper-tropospheric air on the equatorward side of the boundary, not a classic stratospheric intrusion.

In the northwest, a deep purple and magenta region with thick white cloud covers the Pacific Northwest, northern Rockies and the northern Great Basin, and it stretches east-northeastward as a cloud band across Montana and the Dakotas toward the Upper Midwest. The saturated purple suggests cold, dry upper-level air within a trough or closed circulation, with the cloud shield along its leading flank. A second large circulation with a comma-shaped cloud pattern sits over central Canada north of Lake Superior, and a third system is visible at the far northeastern edge of the frame near Newfoundland.

A narrow cloud band extends from the lower Great Lakes across upstate New York and New England, marking a frontal zone along the northern edge of the green moisture. Organized deep convection is limited: the brightest white clusters are over the western Caribbean near the Yucatan, Hispaniola, and Puerto Rico, while thinner cirrus streaks run from south Texas and northeastern Mexico toward the Gulf. The central and eastern U.S. otherwise appears largely clear under green and teal tones.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The most striking feature is the pair of comma-shaped dry-air spirals in the Southern Hemisphere: a compact swirl of saturated orange and red near the lower left (roughly 35 to 40 degrees south over the southeast Pacific, well off the Chilean coast) and a larger, broader spiral off the southern Brazil and Uruguay coast over the southwest Atlantic. Their warm, tightly wound colors on the cyclonic side of the circulation are the classic signature of dry, high-PV stratospheric air being drawn down around cutoff or mature cyclones, with cloud bands wrapping the flanks. Over South America, white cloud clusters stretch from the Colombia and Ecuador border region across northern Brazil, with another batch over eastern Brazil, marking active tropical convection, while a thick cloud shield sits near the Argentine and Uruguayan coast.

In the north, the polar jet corridor is implied by the sharp purple-to-green airmass boundary running across Canada and curving over the Great Lakes toward Newfoundland and the North Atlantic. A tight orange-red comma near the Labrador and Newfoundland sector, with cloud wrapped around it, looks like a cyclone with dry intrusion air on its cyclonic side, and a similar spiral is visible near the far northeast limb. Purple and blue tones over the Arctic and northern Canada indicate cold, dry upper troposphere. A bright cloud mass near the upper right limb of the disk marks a vigorous system in the central Atlantic, though its precise location is uncertain near the edge where viewing angle distorts the geography.

Tropical moisture is broadly green across Mexico, the Caribbean, and the eastern Pacific, with scattered convective clusters over Central America, the Greater Antilles, and the Pacific ITCZ near Panama and Ecuador. A band of cirrus streaks trails northeastward from Mexico and the Gulf region into the Atlantic, consistent with subtropical jet flow, and the broad olive-brown tones over the subtropical Atlantic and Pacific indicate drier subsident air.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
The outlook for November 15-19 favors above-normal temperatures across most of the central and western U.S., with the strongest signal in the northern Plains and Upper Midwest. A core of 80-90% probability stretches from the Dakotas and Minnesota through Iowa, Nebraska and western Wisconsin, with a lobe of 70-80% extending south through Kansas and Oklahoma and 60-70% covering most of Texas, the Rockies and the mid-Mississippi Valley. Probabilities decline steadily toward both coasts, falling to 33-50% (leaning above) across the Pacific Northwest, the interior West and the Ohio Valley.

The cool side is confined to two small areas: a pocket of 33-40% leaning below normal along the central California coast and adjacent Sierra, and a larger swath of 33-40% leaning below from coastal North Carolina through South Carolina, Georgia and all of Florida. Gray near-normal areas sit between these and the warm core, including inland California and Nevada, the central Appalachians and the Northeast coast, plus Alabama and the Georgia interior. Alaska leans above normal, strongest (50-60%) over the eastern interior. Hawaii is also above normal, with probabilities of 50-70%.

The tight packing of the probability contours oriented southwest to northeast across the Ohio Valley and Northeast marks a sharp gradient between the warm interior and the cooler Southeast and Atlantic coast. Probability maps do not show upper-level height or the magnitude of anomalies, so the following is inference. The pattern is consistent with a ridge over the central U.S. and a trough or northerly flow near the East Coast, implied by the cool lean there. The high-confidence warm core argues that this regime persists through at least the middle of the period. Whether it breaks down beyond day 10 cannot be read from this chart, though the weakening probabilities toward the coasts suggest less forecast agreement on the pattern's periphery, particularly on how far east the ridge extends.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly forecast, made 9 Nov 2026 and valid 15-19 Nov. Contours are labeled in meters (5400, 5640, 5820 and so on, i.e. 540-582 dam), and the dashed anomaly lines are in meters at 60 m intervals per the legend. The labels read as plain meters (-30, -90, 150, 210), but the plotted anomaly values look implausibly large for a 5-day mean, with 150 and 210 labels over the eastern interior. That magnitude is far above the few tens of meters (single digits to low double digits in dam) this product normally shows, so I would treat those numbers as probably mislabeled or in different units than they appear, and rely on the pattern and sign rather than the digits.

The dominant feature is a broad positive anomaly center (red dashed) over central and eastern Canada, spanning roughly Manitoba and Ontario to Quebec, extending south across the Great Lakes and northern Plains. A second positive center lies near Baffin Island and the northern Canadian archipelago. Negative anomalies (blue dashed) frame this ridge on both flanks: a trough over the northeast Pacific and Pacific Northwest coast (around -30 to -90), and another over the Atlantic off the northeast U.S. and Canadian Maritimes, with a large negative area over northern Greenland and the Arctic Ocean side.

The ridge axis runs from the central U.S. north-northeast through central Canada toward the Arctic, tilted northeastward, with a closed-looking high near 5280 north of the mainland. The western trough axis sits along or just off the Pacific coast, while the downstream trough is near the Atlantic seaboard. Positive anomalies do not extend into western North America in any meaningful way; the zero line (purple dashed) runs roughly from the Pacific Northwest interior southward through the Rockies and Great Basin, so the West is on the cool, negative side, and the ridge is displaced well to the east of the Rockies.

On amplification, this is a high-amplitude pattern, not a zonal one: contours bow sharply poleward over central Canada and dip equatorward on both coasts. Flow is most zonal only across the southern tier, where contours run west-east near 5760-5880. Since this is a single valid period rather than a sequence, I cannot say from this chart alone whether the western ridge is shrinking or retreating over time; the plotted picture simply shows the positive anomalies centered east of where a western ridge would sit.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb heights and height-anomaly (dashed) outlook, made Nov 9 and valid Nov 17-23, 2026, so the product identification holds. The contour labels read 5160 to about 5820 in meters (516 to 582 dam), and the dashed anomaly lines are labeled at 60 m intervals, so the 30, 90 and 150 labels are meters (roughly 3, 9 and 15 dam). The 90 label sits near the pole and the 150 label over the Great Lakes region, which stretches the plausible scale, so I would treat the exact magnitudes with some doubt.

The strongest positive anomaly is not over western Canada or the northern Rockies. The red dashed anomaly lines enclose a broad positive area covering the Great Lakes, the Ohio Valley and the northeastern U.S., extending into southeastern Canada, with its core near the Great Lakes at roughly 150 m. A second positive center lies over the Arctic Ocean near the pole (about 90 m), under a closed high-height cell. Over western Canada, the northern Rockies and the northern Plains the chart shows no clear positive anomaly; the purple zero line passes through the northern Plains and the dashed contours there are blue, meaning near-normal to modestly negative heights.

Negative anomalies (blue dashed) cover the Pacific Northwest and the western U.S. out into the eastern Pacific, with the largest labeled center near the Southwest and northwestern Mexico at about -60 m. Other negative areas lie near Hudson Bay and Baffin Island and the North Atlantic east of the Canadian Maritimes. The mean height field supports a trough over the western U.S. and eastern Pacific. The implied ridge axis, running north-northeast from the Gulf Coast through the Mississippi Valley toward the Great Lakes, sits well east of the northern Rockies, so the ridge core is displaced eastward and southeastward rather than retreating to the Southwest.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary: This Day 1 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Tuesday Nov 10 through 12Z Wednesday Nov 11, 2026, shows no excessive-rainfall risk anywhere. The chart's own text states that the probability of rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance is less than 5 percent, and no Marginal, Slight, Moderate or High area is drawn over any part of the contiguous United States, the Gulf Coast, Florida or the Atlantic seaboard. With no categories plotted, there is no highest-risk region to identify, and nothing on the chart ties to a tropical system, a stalled front or terrain-enhanced rainfall. The legend is displayed in the lower right, but none of its categories appear on the map. This is a quiet-day product: the absence of risk areas says only that flash-flood-producing rainfall is not expected, not that no rain will fall.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary: This Day 2 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Wednesday 11 November through 12Z Thursday 12 November 2026, has no risk areas drawn anywhere. The lower-48 domain is entirely white, and the overlaid text states that the probability of rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance is less than 5 percent. None of the legend categories (Marginal, Slight, Moderate, High) appear on the map, so no part of the country, from the Pacific coast to the Gulf and Atlantic seaboards, carries even the lowest tier of risk. Because the chart shows only a blanket below-threshold statement, nothing here indicates whether the signal has grown, shifted or relaxed compared with a Day 1 outlook for the same period. The product speaks only to flash-flood-guidance exceedance, so it does not rule out ordinary rain or snow, only rainfall heavy enough to cause flash flooding.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: As of 3 AM EST Tue Nov 10, 2026: Heavy rain over southern Texas is easing as an upper low moves east, with showers lingering along the western and central Gulf Coast. Pacific systems bring moderate rain and higher-elevation snow to the Pacific Northwest, heaviest on the Olympic Peninsula (a few inches through Thursday). Clippers bring scattered showers to the Great Lakes and Northeast through Wednesday. A low from the northern Plains reaches the Appalachians by Thursday morning, intensifying and spreading strong winds across the eastern half of the country. Embedded thunderstorms and gusty winds hit the Midwest, Ohio and Tennessee Valleys Wednesday. A cold airmass surges east Wednesday night into Thursday, bringing wet snow to the upper Great Lakes by Thursday morning. The West stays milder than normal and mostly dry outside the Northwest. Frost advisories cover eastern North Carolina and southeastern Virginia this morning, and mild air reaches the East Coast this afternoon.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
Issued 6:36 AM CST Tuesday, November 10, 2026, valid through 12Z November 11. No severe thunderstorm areas are forecast, and organized severe storms are not expected through tonight.

Elevated thunderstorms may persist for much of the period along coastal Texas and Louisiana as a weak mid-level shortwave trough moves east across the southern Plains into the lower Mississippi Valley. MUCAPE should stay generally below 1000 J/kg with modest lapse rates aloft, so any hail from stronger cells that form over land should remain sub-severe.

Separately, low-topped convection moving quickly east-northeast across coastal Washington today, tied to another mid-level shortwave, may produce occasional lightning. Very weak instability limits the severe threat there.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No SPC mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours. No organized convective threat is currently being actively monitored by the Storm Prediction Center.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic (as of 700 AM EST, Tue Nov 10, 2026): Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the North Atlantic, Caribbean Sea, or Gulf of America during the next 7 days.

East Pacific (as of 400 AM PST, Tue Nov 10, 2026): The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Tropical Storm Pena, located several hundred miles south-southwest of Honolulu, Hawaii. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected elsewhere in the eastern and central North Pacific east of 180 degrees longitude during the next 7 days.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary:
Tropical Storm Pena, as of 0900 UTC November 10, 2026 (1100 PM HST November 9), is centered near 11.7N 163.9W, about 510 miles southeast of Johnston Island and 770 miles south-southwest of Honolulu. It is moving west (270 degrees) at 14 mph. Maximum sustained winds are 40 mph (35 kt) with higher gusts, and the estimated minimum central pressure is 1004 mb. Tropical-storm-force winds extend up to 125 miles from the center. A recent scatterometer pass showed an elongated, asymmetric wind field, strongest in the northeast quadrant.

There are no coastal watches or warnings, and no hazards affecting land.

Intensity: Little change is forecast over the next few days, though fluctuations are possible. Moderate south-southwesterly shear and possibly drier mid-level air limit strengthening. Shear is expected to ease over the next 12 to 24 hours, but only a few intensity models show modest strengthening. Sea surface temperatures near 29 C persist along the track. Drier mid-level air arriving around 60 hours and strengthening shear late in the period should inhibit intensification. Pena could degenerate into a remnant low or open into a trough, especially later in the forecast period.

Track: Motion is expected to stay westward for about 48 hours as a ridge builds to the north. The center should pass several hundred nautical miles south of Johnston Atoll. A gradual turn west-northwest is expected afterward as a weakness develops in the ridge. The track was shifted south from the previous forecast. Forecast positions are 11.2N 167.7W at 24 hours, 11.3N 173.3W at 48 hours, 12.3N 179.4W at 72 hours, and 13.5N 171.1E at 120 hours.

The next complete advisory is due at 500 AM HST.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary:
The Oceanic Niño Index shows a strengthening El Niño. The latest value, for the ASO 2026 season, is +2.46°C, well above the +0.5°C El Niño threshold and in the strong category (+2.0°C and above).

The index has risen every season, from -0.21°C in JFM 2026 (a cool-neutral reading) through +0.11°C in FMA, +0.46°C in MAM, and +0.95°C in AMJ. It then climbed to +1.39°C in MJJ, +1.80°C in JJA, +2.16°C in JAS, and +2.46°C in ASO. The rise has been steady and has accelerated since spring, with the most recent gains of about 0.3°C per season.

The TOTAL column shows the underlying seasonal sea surface temperature, which climbed from 26.57 to 29.23 over the same period. The product does not state an as-of date.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
Teleconnection indices from NOAA CPC, observed values as of 2026-10-31. The table is flagged stale: CPC has not updated it, and the newest value is 10 days old, so none of these readings should be treated as current. Extratropical teleconnections are weaker outside winter, so use these only as directional support.

PNA: latest +0.57, positive, which favors western North American ridging with eastern troughing. The 7-day mean fell to -0.24 from +0.06 (-0.30). Daily values dipped to about -0.58 for several days before recovering to positive at the end of the period.

AO: latest +0.77, positive, which does not favor high-latitude blocking. The 7-day mean fell to +1.03 from +1.44 (-0.41). Values were strongly positive early in the period (+2.71, +2.78) and have declined since.

NAO: latest +1.15, positive. The 7-day mean rose to +0.59 from +0.26 (+0.33). Values were negative in mid-period (near -0.79) and have climbed back to positive.
